authors: Pérez Montes, C.; García Villasur, J.; Gutiérrez de Rozas, L.; Jiménez, G.; Lavín, N.; Matyunina, A.; Vegas, R.
title: The impact of the autumn 2024 flash floods in Spain from a financial stability standpoint
venue: Banco de España Financial Stability Review 48, pp. 5-40
verified: 2026-11-02 via Banco de España PDF + Crossref
question: Size and quality of bank exposures in areas hit by the Oct 2024 Valencia floods; did credit, stage 2 and stage 3 diverge afterwards?
data: Copernicus flood geolocation + Central Credit Register (CIRBE) + Cadastre (geolocated real-estate collateral); Sep 2024-Feb 2025
identification: Borrower-level DiD; treatment = postcodes of RDL 6/2024 municipalities (borrower or collateral); PSM control from Mediterranean-coast postcodes; firm/household, sector x time and main-bank x time FE
main_finding: Firms: stage 2 share +~0.5 pp Dec 2024-Jan 2025 (+4.5% rel.), NPL +3.4% rel. from Jan 2025 (pp. 19-20). Households: stage 2 +0.45 pp in Dec only (+4.1%), stage 3 +0.44 pp (+9.1%) (p. 21). Banks with >40% of credit in affected areas: stage 2 to affected firms +24%, stage 3 -9% (p. 21). Authors note moratoria may have flattered credit quality (p. 17).
how_my_project_differs: First evidence that floods surface in stage 2 and that exposed banks shift stage 3 into stage 2 under relief (H-S5a); project adds an emerging market with thin insurance, national-scale event, satellite intensity, LGD and collateral values, multi-year horizon

authors: Guo, W.; Miao, Q.; Kim, Y.; Hou, Y.
title: Rising Waters, Falling Taxes: The Impact of Hurricane Sandy on Property Tax Assessments in New York City
venue: Working paper (23 June 2025), PDF hosted at brookings.edu
read_depth: full text, results sections, not cover-to-cover (Sections 1, 3.4, 5.1-5.2)
question: Did Sandy change official property assessments and tax burdens for inundated homes and for undamaged homes in high-risk zones?
data: NYC Department of Finance assessment rolls and property sales, Class 1 residential
identification: DiD inundated vs non-inundated; Zone A x post for non-inundated homes
main_finding: Inundated: sale price -10%, assessor market value -17% (mostly tax relief), assessed value -10%, taxable value -6.5% (Table 3, pp. 22-23). Non-inundated Zone A: sale price -11% but no change in assessor market, assessed or taxable values (Table 4, p. 24). Assessment caps (6%/yr, 20%/5 yrs) blunt transmission.
how_my_project_differs: Counter-example to 'no study of official values'; project studies official appraisals that anchor bank collateral (Thai Treasury), ex-ante satellite hazard, in an emerging market

authors: Sawada, Y.; Nakata, H.; Sekiguchi, K.
title: Natural Disasters, Land Price, and Location of Firms: Evidence from Thailand
read_depth: full for Section 3 (land prices); abstract and intro; Section 2 skimmed
question: Did 2011 flood awareness shape firm location, and did the floods move land prices?
data: RIETI firm survey (185 Thai responses); JETRO industrial-estate land prices, 10 rounds Oct 2008-Nov 2012, 7 flooded IEs; AREA price series in 43 districts
identification: DiD with IE or district FE; flooded provinces treated
main_finding: IE land prices in flooded estates ~10% of mean lower relative to non-flooded (-337.9, 10% level; Table 10), driven by rises elsewhere; AREA: industrial land -1,025 and townhouses -71,456 relative, residential and commercial land insignificant (Table 12)
how_my_project_differs: Uses survey/broker price series, not official appraisals; province-level treatment; project uses parcel-level Treasury appraisals and satellite exposure

authors: Nie, O.; Regelink, M.; Wang, D.
title: Banking Sector Risk in the Aftermath of Climate Change and Environmental-Related Natural Disasters
venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 10326
question: Effect of climate-related disasters on system-wide NPLs, cross-country and in the Philippines
data: 184 countries over ~40 years; Philippine regional banking data 2011-2018
identification: Local projections; regional panel for typhoon damage/GDP
main_finding: Severe disasters raise system-wide NPLs persistently; in the Philippines a 1 pp rise in typhoon damage/regional GDP raises the NPL ratio by up to 2.3% (p. 5)
how_my_project_differs: Aggregate and regional; project is loan/collateral-level with PD, LGD and staging

authors: Brei, M.; Mohan, P.; Perez Barahona, A.; Strobl, E.
title: Transmission of natural disasters to the banking sector: Evidence from thirty years of tropical storms in the Caribbean
venue: Journal of International Money and Finance 141:103008
question: Channels through which tropical storms affect banks in small and continental emerging economies
data: 92 damaging tropical storms; 111 banks in 20 Caribbean and Central American jurisdictions
main_finding: Immediate and lasting funding shocks; lending to the private sector drops; persistent loan defaults and losses in continental countries, while in small islands losses appear only after four years; credit-less recovery
how_my_project_differs: Bank-level and storms; project is loan/collateral-level floods with relief-censored default and staging

title: 2024 Climate Risk Stress Testing Exercise: Methodology Paper
read_depth: full for Part C2 (pp. 23-24); contents and keyword search of the rest
question: Supervisory specification of Malaysia's first industry-wide climate stress test
data: Institutions' own portfolios as of 31 Dec 2023
identification: Forward scenario: one-off nationwide 1-in-200-year flood under RCP 8.5 (2050 climate)
main_finding: Postcode-level hazard at minimum; property and construction loans at minimum; banks must assume no government policy interventions; macro-driven models may be insensitive to localised flood losses (S 14.1-15.1)
how_my_project_differs: Forward, not reverse; assumes away relief, whereas the project models relief explicitly and inverts for the breaking severity

authors: Pozdyshev, V.; Lobanov, A.; Ilinsky, K.
title: Incorporating physical climate risks into banks' credit risk models
question: How to integrate physical risk into credit risk models
identification: Extension of one-factor Vasicek model with a climate-event state and state-dependent LGD
main_finding: In the illustration, LGD rises from 10% to 24.8% in the climate state and unexpected loss from 0.0069 to 0.0744 (p. 29)
how_my_project_differs: Theory/modelling only; possible building block for the RQ3 loss model

authors: Fontana, A.; Jarmulska, B.; Scheid, B.; Scheins, C.; Schwarz, C.
title: From flood to fire: is physical climate risk taken into account in banks' residential mortgage rates?
question: Do euro-area banks price physical climate risk into mortgage rates?
data: Euro-area residential mortgage data (details not read)
main_finding: Banks on average charge a physical-risk premium that has risen; banks judged adequate in the ECB thematic review charge more
how_my_project_differs: Pricing of hazard, not staging, PD or LGD; advanced economy

authors: Fitzmaurice, K. P.; Garcia, H. M.; Sebastian, A.; Thomson, H.; Zeff, H. B.; Characklis, G. W.
title: Flood risks to the financial stability of residential mortgage borrowers: an integrated modeling approach
venue: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences 26:675-701
question: How many flood-exposed mortgage borrowers face credit constraints from negative equity or illiquidity?
identification: Simulation of damage, property value and mortgage balance
main_finding: USD 4.0 bn damage, 66% uninsured; 48% of affected mortgage borrowers insured; 32% lacked income or collateral to finance repairs
how_my_project_differs: US simulation; project estimates realised LGD/collateral effects empirically in an emerging market

authors: Albertazzi, U.; Djekic, D.; Ponte Marques, A.
title: Physical climate risk, credit risk and lending activity
read_depth: full text, results sections, not cover-to-cover (Sections 1-3, 5.3, Table 17, opening of 6)
question: Causal effect of floods on lending, rates, collateral requirements and default of pre-existing loans
data: AnaCredit loans >=EUR 25,000 located by borrower registered address + Copernicus EMS maps; four floods 2021-2024; ECB 0-5 hazard indicator (RCP 4.5)
identification: Spatial RD at flood boundary (local linear, triangular kernel, CCT bandwidths ~360-460 m); firm-time FE for supply vs demand
main_finding: Default ratio +0.568 pp after one quarter (10% level; Table 8, p. 27) and +0.64-0.69 pp over two quarters (Table 9, p. 28), ~doubling a 1.4% annual rate; 0.4-0.9 pp across bandwidths. Real-estate-backed micro-firm loans: LTV +5.3 pp, large-firm interaction -6.2 pp (Table 17, p. 39)
how_my_project_differs: Borrower address not collateral location; no LGD or staging; insured/aided advanced economies; project adds collateral-level exposure, LGD, staging and relief censoring

title: Flood risk and financial stability: Evidence from a stress test for the Netherlands
read_depth: full text, results sections, not cover-to-cover (Sections 1 and 5)
question: How much would floods of increasing severity deplete Dutch banks' capital?
data: Geocoded real-estate collateral of ten banks (>95% of sector assets) matched to flood inundation scenarios
identification: Scenario stress test with PD/LGD modules; six scenarios (1, 3, 5 m; unprotected vs protected areas); self-described as 'in essence' a reverse stress test
main_finding: CET1 -110 bp (1 m) to -132 bp (5 m) in unprotected areas (p. 22); protected west -307 bp (1 m), ~-400 bp (3 m), -712 bp (5 m) (p. 23); residential damage contributes 402 bp in the extreme case via LGD and RWA (p. 24)
how_my_project_differs: Modelled hazard, scenario escalation rather than formal inversion; insured, protected advanced economy; project estimates elasticities from realised floods and solves for the breaking severity under relief

title: High water, no marks? Biased lending after extreme weather
read_depth: full text, results sections, not cover-to-cover (WP version: Section 3 data, Sections 4.1-4.3.1)
question: Do lender valuations and mortgage terms track local price falls after floods?
data: 38,747 refinanced mortgages around the 2013-14 English winter floods; EA flood outlines and 2013-14 hazard-map update
identification: Repeat-transaction DiD with postcode-district x year FE; matched samples
main_finding: Prolonged flooding lowers sale prices 4.2% (full), 3.3% (matched), 2.6% (controls); refinancing valuation differential +3.2%/+2.9%; rate effects (31/21 bp) not robust to matching; loan amounts unaffected (Tables 3 and 5, pp. 22-24); lenders index valuations too coarsely
how_my_project_differs: Lender valuations, insured setting, no default/LGD/provisioning; project tests official appraisals that anchor collateral and links them to LGD and staging

authors: Noy, I.; Nguyen, C.; Patel, P.
title: Floods and Spillovers: Households after the 2011 Great Flood in Thailand
venue: Economic Development and Cultural Change 69(2):829-868 (CESifo WP 7644)
read_depth: full text, results sections, not cover-to-cover (WP version: data, Section 5 text, conclusions; tables not read)
question: Direct and spillover effects of the 2011 Thai flood on household income, spending, assets, debt and savings
data: Thai SES waves with 2012 flood module; GISTDA weekly satellite images May-Dec 2011 at 50 x 50 m (flooded sub-districts, duration <2 or >2 weeks)
identification: DiD on repeated cross-sections; direct vs spillover households; placebo years
main_finding: Business income falls THB 6,465 (direct) and THB 4,018 (spillover) (Section 5.3, p. 26); total spending unchanged, housing up, luxuries down; longer floods roughly double income effects; debt and savings effects small and insignificant (unreported; pp. 22-23)
how_my_project_differs: Households not loans; no usable debt result; project uses loan/collateral outcomes, and GISTDA 50 m duration data are a candidate 2011 exposure source
